U.S. NEWS THE OUTLOOK | By Matt Grossman and Anthony DeBarros # Why Higher Bond Yields Aren't Going Away Some economic shocks look like bumps in the road—tariffs, to which businesses adjust, or a war with Iran that raises oil prices temporarily. But economists increasingly believe that higher U.S. interest rates will define the rest of the decade. So concludes The Wall Street Journal's latest survey of forecasters. The surveyed analysts don't see the recent surge in long-term yields to quarter-century highs as a temporary slip that will ease as inflation cools. Instead, they expect higher long-term yields to be sustained. Treasuries set the tempo for borrowing costs across the economy. Higher yields mean higher mortgage rates and more expensive borrowing for companies. They also increase the burden on the federal budget, where interest on the national debt now exceeds military spending. The 71 analysts who submitted projections in the survey from Oct. 2-7 now expect the benchmark 10-year yield to end 2026 at 5.1%, up from 4.9% in 2025. When we asked, in July. Not all respondents answered every question. Higher yields are expected to railset. Forecasters see a 10-year yield of 4.96% halfway through 2027 and 4.78% at the end of 2027, up from 4.3% and 4.26% in July projections. A mix of improving growth, inflation and concerns about the U.S. fiscal trajectory have pushed bond yields higher since the start of the summer. Many economists said the cocktail has forced them to re-evaluate assumptions about demand for Treasuries, whose yields rise when their prices fall. "It has been a sea change in the fundamentals underlying the fixed-income market and the economy," Allen Sinai, president of consulting firm Decision Economics, said in an interview. He said even after the Federal Reserve's interest-rate increase last month, the central bank has fallen behind in the battle to tame inflation. Sinai said it would take more than one hike to smother inflation, which the Fed appeared to acknowledge with its September projections. Those showed the Fed's short-term interest-rate target, the federal-funds rate, topping 4% this year and staying there through 2027. Sinai forecasts the 10-year yield could rise to nearly 6% next year and remain above 5% through the 2020s. Yields on Treasury securities are heavily influenced by investors' expectations for how the Fed will set interest rates in coming years. Much of the recent increase in inflation is because of higher oil prices, which economists expect to recede. They forecast the U.S. oil-price benchmark will end the year at $88 a barrel, compared with$91.85 on Friday, and slip below $80 by July. As a result, they expect inflation as measured by the consumer-price index of 3.5% in December, 2.6% next June, and 2.3% at the end of 2027. That has changed little from three months ago. The inflation gauge that the Fed tracks, the personal-consumption expenditures price index, is forecast to cool to 2.4% at the end of 2027, from 3.5% at the end of this year. Carl Tannenbaum, chief economist at Chicago-based Northern Trust, said factors beyond the inflation outlook have pushed up expected yields. Inflationary pressure from the Iran war could abate if the conflict winds down, which would help ease yields, all else equal, he said. But investors will remain nervous about the large and growing debt burden, while the AI infrastructure build-out could lift growth expectations and demand for capital, Tannenbaum said. He sees the 10-year yield around 5.2% through 2028, before falling to 5% by the end of 2029. Yields at that level would strain the federal budget. In February, the Congressional Budget Office projected the 10-year Treasury yield won't exceed 4.3% for the rest of the decade. The White House Office of Management and Budget is even more optimistic, projecting yields falling into the mid-3% range later this decade. Economists penicled in higher expected growth this year. They expect GDP to increase by 2.4% in 2026, up from their 2.1% July projection. That reflects upward revisions to second-quarter growth and interim data suggesting the economy might have grown by an annualized rate of more than 3% in the third quarter. Respondents see growth slipping back thereafter, to 2.1% or 2.2% for the rest of the decade. Likewise, forecasters don't anticipate much drama in the labor market. On average, they think unemployment will hang around 4.2% through 2029, little changed from the 4.2% unemployment rate in September. They put the probability of recession in the coming 12 months at 24%, barely below the 25% rate. Not all forecasters agree yields will stay high. Rajeev Dhawan, an economist at Georgia State University, thinks the labor market is more fragile than it appears. Over the past six months, the economy has added a solid 66,000 jobs a month on average, but few have been in the most lucrative fields, he said. In Dhawan's view, a weaker labor market could force the Fed to bring rates lower again, which could pull down yields. "The labor market's got a white-collar job malaise," Dhawan said. "Once the Fed realizes it isn't as strong, they will pivot to rate cuts." # Fed's Hammack Sees Engine of Inflation on Factory Floor By Nick Timraos CLEVELAND—Jack Schron spent most of 90 minutes last week showing Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack how good business has gotten at Jergens, a family-run manufacturer built on the site of old railroad buildings on the city's east side. Jack Schron and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack during a tour of Jergens in Cleveland. Orders from aerospace companies are surging, tariffs have made a Chinese rival's parts more expensive, and the company is about to make the biggest machine-tool purchase in its 84-year history. Jergens makes industrial hardware such as clamps and quick-release pins that lock everything from aircraft panels to concert speakers into position. What matters most to his customers has shifted, Schron told the central banker. Quality is still the minimum for getting in the door, the aerospace giants. "The next threshold used to be price," he said. Now it is speed. "No one wants to go to anything anymore," said Schron, the company's president. Buyers will pay a premium to get products in weeks instead of months, and that has helped Jergens' bottom line. That kind of pricing power worries inflation fighters like Hammack. It suggests demand is outrunning what suppliers can make, a dynamic that higher interest rates are supposed to tamp down. Yet interest rates never came up during her visit, which ended with a ton of the busy factory floor. Jergens is one company, but its experience fits what Hammack said she is hearing from across her district. "You heard it from Jack. He's buying expensive machinery. He's investing. He sees a lot of demand. The growth is there," Hammack said in an interview after the tour. It is a big reason she thinks the Fed, which raised its benchmark rate last month to a range of 3.75% to 4%, needs to go higher still. With inflation above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years, Hammack says she hears from lower-income households that are no longer just trading down at the grocery store but choosing which bills to pay. Most of her colleagues last month saw inflation returning to target in 2029. "To me, that's far too long," she said. Hammack, who spent more than 30 years at Goldman Sachs before joining the Fed in 2024, has been among the most outspoken officials in pushing for higher rates. "I grew up in a world as a trader where if I was wrong 40% of the time, that was a pretty good day, so I'm not afraid of putting out a forecast," she said. Hammack was early to argue that rates might not be restraining the economy as much as Fed officials thought, and the boom in AI-related spending rippling through the industrial and technology sectors has since brought more of her colleagues around to that view. The question now is how quickly to adjust. Minutes of the Fed's September meeting showed most officials thought another increase would likely be appropriate by year-end, and several have signaled they think the Fed doesn't need to raise rates again this month. Hammack didn't sound as patient. "Smaller, more frequent adjustments are preferable to larger" ones, in part because making bigger moves can be harder for businesses to prepare for, said Hammack. In July, when the Fed held rates steady, she was one of three policymakers who dissented in favor of a rate increase. Officials often gauge how much they are restraining the economy against some estimate of an unobservable "neutral" rate, the level that neither spurs nor slows growth. Hammack said her estimate is among the highest on the committee, and that if she is wrong, it is too low. "When you see the amount of capital that's flowing in, when you see the profits that are being created, to me, this does not look like an economy that has restraint," she said. Long-term Treasury yields have been on the march since the summer, raising borrowing costs across the economy. Hammack said that has moved financial conditions closer to neutral, but she rejected the suggestion that the bond market could do the Fed's work for it. "Absolutely not," she said. "It's not a substitute, it's a complement." Outside the Fed, critics argue that higher rates are the wrong tool for the job. They can't produce more oil and may not immediately slow AI spending financed by tech giants' cash and the bond market. Hammack conceded the point. "I do not think that raising rates is going to materially slow the data-center demand," she said. Hammack's willingness to say where she stands sets her apart from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. Warsh has said he wants to move the Fed away from signaling its own moves or narrating its forecasts, which he has argued locks officials into defending a projection instead of responding to the economy as it unfolds. Saying less just leaves businesses and households to guess, Hammack said. Her job is to "arm the public with as much information as possible" and to "treat them like mature grown-ups." # CORRECTIONS & AMPLIFICATIONS Readers can alert The Wall Street Journal to any errors in news articles by emailing corrections@wallstreet.com or by calling 888-762-5450.
